item.title: Access tokens and refresh tokens
item.description: Why token-based login splits access tokens from refresh tokens, and where each token is kept and how it is refreshed.
item.content:encoded:
The previous post said that with tokens the server stores nothing, so it can’t invalidate a token it has already issued. This post looks at splitting tokens into access tokens and refresh tokens to reduce that problem, and at where to keep the two tokens and how to refresh them.

The examples assume the page and the API are on the same origin. If they’re on different origins, the settings in the cookies post are also needed.

Why two tokens

A single token lifetime is hard to get right.

Lifetime Upside Problem
Long (e.g. 14 days) Users don’t have to log in again A leaked token can be used by someone else for 14 days
Short (e.g. 30 minutes) A leaked token is useless after 30 minutes Users have to log in again every 30 minutes

So two tokens with different jobs are used.

Access token Refresh token
Job Proves the user on API requests Gets a new access token
Sent to Every API request Only the refresh request (/auth/refresh)
Lifetime Short (e.g. 15–30 minutes) Long (e.g. 1–2 weeks)
Format Usually a JWT A JWT or a long random string
Stored on the server No Yes (database, Redis)
  • The access token travels with every request, so it has many chances to leak. In exchange its lifetime is short, so a leak does damage only briefly.
  • The refresh token is sent only when refreshing, so it has few chances to leak. Because the server stores it, deleting it on the server makes it unusable immediately.

Since the refresh token is stored on the server, this approach adds some of the benefits of sessions to tokens. Requests don’t need a store lookup (access token), while logout is handled on the server (refresh token).

There’s no single right lifetime. A shorter access token means less damage if it leaks but more refresh requests; a longer refresh token means fewer logins but a longer window in which a leaked token can be used.

Sending tokens

There are two ways to send a token to the server.

Authorization header Cookie
Who adds it The page code, on every request The browser, automatically
Does the page code need to hold the token Yes No (with HttpOnly it can’t even read it)
Is it attached to requests sent by other sites No It can be (blocked with SameSite)

As in the previous post, how the token is sent is chosen separately from whether you use sessions or tokens. A JWT can be sent in a cookie too.

Where to store tokens

On login you receive an access token and a refresh token, and you have to decide where in the browser to keep each. The options are localStorage, browser memory and an HttpOnly cookie.

Keeping something in browser memory means not writing it to browser storage, only to a JavaScript variable in the code running in the open tab. It isn’t on the server. When the page reloads or the tab closes, the code starts over and the value is gone.

Where Is it memory
A module variable (let accessToken), React state, a Zustand store Memory
A Zustand store using persist Not memory. persist saves the value to localStorage

Where a token is kept determines how dangerous an attack becomes.

XSS and CSRF

A token becomes dangerous in two ways. Both are attacks from the cookies post.

The token is stolen (XSS): If an attacker hides a script in a post’s content, the script runs in the browser of any user who opens that post. The script reads the token and sends it to the attacker’s server.

The attacker then calls the API from their own computer with that token, acting as the user until the token expires.

The token is used without the user knowing (CSRF): The browser adds cookies to requests automatically. If the user opens the attacker’s site while logged in, that site can make a request to our server, and the user’s cookie goes with it. The attacker never learns the token’s value, but uses the token through the user’s browser.

Comparing storage locations

Location Stolen (XSS) Used without the user knowing (CSRF) After a reload
localStorage Scripts can read it Not sent automatically, so not applicable Kept
Memory The variable is hard to reach Not applicable Gone
HttpOnly cookie Scripts can’t read it Sent automatically, so it must be blocked with SameSite and so on Kept

Each has trade-offs, so the two tokens go in different places.

Where each token goes

The refresh token goes in an HttpOnly cookie. It’s valid for a long time, say 14 days, so if it’s stolen, new access tokens can be obtained for that whole period. So it goes in an HttpOnly cookie that scripts can’t read, and cookie attributes block it from being used without the user knowing.

  • SameSite=Strict: the cookie isn’t sent with requests that start from another site.
  • Path=/auth: the cookie is sent only with refresh and logout requests, not with other API requests.

The access token goes in memory or localStorage. The page code has to put it in the Authorization header of every request, so it has to be somewhere the code can read. In exchange it’s short-lived, say 30 minutes, so a stolen one is useless 30 minutes later.

Memory localStorage
Stealing it Hard Easy
Reload, new tab Gone, so it has to be fetched again with a refresh request Still there, used right away

No storage location stops XSS itself. While a script is running, it can send requests as the user even without reading the token. XSS is prevented by never inserting user input into HTML as is, and by limiting which scripts may run with a CSP (Content Security Policy) header.

CORS settings

The attacker’s site can also make the user’s browser call our server’s /auth/refresh. The attacker’s site and our server are different sites, so a SameSite=Strict cookie isn’t sent. Even with a setting that lets the cookie go along, the browser doesn’t show the response holding the new access token to the attacker’s site, because reading a response from another origin requires the server’s permission through CORS.

This protection holds only while the server allows CORS narrowly. If it allows every origin and also sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, the attacker’s site can read the response and take the new access token.

The CORS setting depends on where the page and the API live.

Page and API CORS setting
Same origin (Nginx or a dev server proxy forwards /api and /auth) Not needed. Leave it unset
Different origins (app.example.com and api.example.com) Allow only the page’s address

With different origins, list the origins to allow. In Spring:

With Spring Security, this setting is applied with http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()).

An example setup

The examples in this post put everything above together like this.

Item Setup
Refresh token HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict; Path=/auth cookie
Access token Browser memory (a JavaScript variable). Fetched again from /auth/refresh after a reload
CORS Unset on the same origin; on different origins, allow only the page’s address
XSS Never insert user input into HTML as is, and set a CSP header

The access token also works in localStorage. That saves a refresh request on every reload, but if XSS happens, the token can be taken and used for the rest of its lifetime.

This is one way of setting things up where the page code handles the access token itself; there are others.

Setup What the browser holds Characteristics
This post’s setup Access token (memory), refresh token (HttpOnly cookie) The page code handles the access token
Both tokens in HttpOnly cookies Two cookies The page code never touches a token. Every API request needs CSRF protection
BFF (Backend for Frontend) One session cookie A server dedicated to the page keeps the tokens and calls the API on its behalf. No token in the browser, but one more server
Sessions A session ID cookie No tokens. Covered in the previous post

Refreshing tokens

When the access token expires, the API returns 401. On that 401, the page code gets a new access token with the refresh token and sends the failed request again.

If the refresh request fails too, the refresh token has also expired, so the user is sent to the login page.

Issuing and refreshing in Spring

  • The access token goes in the response body; the refresh token goes in Set-Cookie.
  • @CookieValue reads a value from the request’s cookies. The refresh token is HttpOnly, so the page code never knows its value; the browser sends it as a cookie.
  • jwtProvider.createAccessToken is the JWT issuing code from the previous post.

Refresh token rotation

rotate above checks the refresh token it receives, deletes it from the store and issues a new refresh token. Replacing the refresh token on every refresh like this is called refresh token rotation.

If a refresh token leaks and two people hold the same token, one of them refreshes first, and the other then sends a token that has already been deleted. When a deleted token comes back, the server can treat it as a sign that someone copied the token, delete all of that user’s refresh tokens and make them log in again.

Refreshing with axios

This example keeps the access token in memory. The refresh request goes through an instance with no interceptors. If it went through the same instance, a 401 on the refresh request would trigger another refresh, over and over.

This code only shows the flow. If the page sends several requests at once and they all get 401, several refresh requests go out too. With rotation, every refresh request after the first sends a token that has already been deleted, so in practice the other requests need to wait until the refresh finishes.

With the access token in memory, it’s gone after a reload, so call auth.post('/refresh') once when the app starts to get an access token.

Logout

Logging out means making both tokens unusable.

Token On logout
Refresh token Deleted from the server’s store, and from the browser with a Max-Age=0 cookie
Access token Cleared from memory (or localStorage) by the page code

The Set-Cookie that deletes the cookie must have the same Path as when it was created to be treated as the same cookie.

The server can’t invalidate an access token it has already issued, so anyone who copied it can use it for the rest of its lifetime. That’s why access tokens are kept short-lived. If they must be blocked immediately, the server can keep a list of blocked tokens and check it on every request, but then every request needs a store lookup, which makes it much like sessions.

Summary

Access token Refresh token
Job Proves the user on API requests Gets a new access token
Lifetime Short Long
How it’s sent Authorization header Cookie (Path=/auth)
Where the browser keeps it Memory or localStorage HttpOnly cookie
Stored on the server No Yes
When it expires Get a new one with the refresh token Log in again
Logout Cleared on the page; usable for the rest of its lifetime Deleted on the server; unusable immediately

That covers the flow of tokens as seen from the page. How the server checks the token on every request and returns 401 or 403 is the subject of the next post, which implements it with Spring Security.

Making concurrent requests that all get 401 wait so the token is refreshed only once is covered with axios interceptors in the API responses and error handling series.

item.title: Sessions and tokens
item.description: How sessions and tokens, the two ways a server recognises a user after login, differ and how each one works.
item.content:encoded:
The previous post looked at cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage, the places a browser stores values. This post looks at how sessions and tokens, the two ways a server recognises a user after login, differ and how each one works.

The backend examples use Spring Boot.

Authentication and authorization

Login involves two separate jobs.

Meaning Example
Authentication Checking who sent the request Checking that the username and password match
Authorization Checking whether that person may do this Only admins can see the user list

Authentication comes first; authorization happens once you know who it is. The status codes for failure differ too. A failed authentication returns 401, and an authenticated user without permission gets 403. The difference between the two codes is in the HTTP status codes post.

The sessions and tokens in this post are about authentication, specifically how a user who has logged in once is recognised again on the next request.

HTTP and login state

HTTP is stateless. Once the server answers a request, it doesn’t remember it, and treats the next request as if it had never seen the sender before.

Even if login succeeds in request 1, request 2 carries nothing that says “this is the person who sent request 1”. So when login succeeds, the server gives the browser a credential, and the browser sends it with every request after that.

The approaches differ in what that credential is.

Approach Credential Where the user’s details live
Sessions A session ID (a meaningless random string) On the server
Tokens A token (a signed string holding the user’s details) Inside the token

Session-based login

A session is space where the server keeps the details of a logged-in user. The server gives each session a session ID, and hands only the session ID to the browser.

  1. The browser sends the username and password.
  2. The server checks them, creates a session and stores the user’s details in the session store.
  3. The server sends the session ID with Set-Cookie in the response.
  4. The browser sends the session ID as a cookie with every later request. The page code does nothing extra.
  5. The server finds the user’s details in the session store by the session ID.

A session ID like a1b2c3 means nothing on its own. In practice it is a random value long enough that it can’t be guessed. Who is logged in is recorded only in the server’s session store.

Sessions in Spring

Spring Boot’s embedded Tomcat keeps sessions in server memory and sends the session ID in a cookie named JSESSIONID. The example below handles the session directly to show the flow. With Spring Security, checking the login and storing the session are done for you.

The session cookie’s attributes and how long a session lasts are set in the configuration file.

timeout counts from the last request. As long as the user keeps sending requests, the session stays; after 30 minutes with no requests, the user is logged out.

Token-based login

With tokens, the server doesn’t store a session. Instead it puts the user’s details in a single string, adds a signature only the server can produce, and gives that to the browser. That string is the token.

  1. The browser sends the username and password.
  2. The server checks them, then creates a token holding the user’s details and signs it.
  3. The server sends the token in the response body.
  4. The browser keeps the token and puts it in the Authorization header of every later request.
  5. The server checks that the token’s signature is valid and uses the user’s details from the token as is.

Authorization is the HTTP header for sending credentials, and Bearer is the name of the scheme, meaning “whoever holds this token”. Unlike cookies, the browser doesn’t add it automatically, so the page code adds it to every request. The request interceptor in the fetch and axios post is an example of doing that.

There are several token formats; the most widely used on the web is JWT.

JWT structure

A JWT (JSON Web Token) is made of three parts separated by dots (.).

Part Contents
Header The signing algorithm. HS256 signs and verifies with a single secret key
Payload The data in the token. Each item is called a claim
Signature A value computed from the header and payload with the server’s secret key

Claims that often go in the payload:

Claim Meaning Example
sub Who the token belongs to (subject), usually the user ID "42"
iat When it was issued (issued at), in seconds since 1970 1791968400 (2026-10-14 18:00 KST)
exp When it expires (expiration) 1791970200 (2026-10-14 18:30 KST)

You can also add claims of your own, such as role.

Signature

The signature is a value computed from the header and payload with a secret key only the server knows. When the server receives a token, it runs the same computation again and checks that the result matches the token’s signature.

If someone changes role in the payload to ADMIN, the signature has to be recomputed to match. Without the secret key, a matching signature can’t be produced. So a token with a valid signature can be trusted to be exactly what the server issued, and the server uses the details in it without looking anything up in a session store.

The signature only shows whether the token was changed; it doesn’t hide the contents. The header and payload are just characters converted with Base64URL, so anyone who converts them back can read the JSON. That’s why passwords and personal information don’t go in the payload.

JWTs in Spring

Libraries for creating and verifying JWTs in Spring include jjwt and Nimbus JOSE + JWT (used by Spring Security). The example below uses jjwt 0.12.

parseSignedClaims throws when the signature doesn’t match or exp has passed. In practice, a filter runs this check on every request and returns 401 when it fails.

The secret key doesn’t go in the code; it comes in through an environment variable or a configuration server. If the secret key leaks, anyone can produce a valid signature.

Sessions and tokens compared

Sessions Tokens (JWT)
What the server stores A session per logged-in user Nothing (just the secret key)
On each request Look up the session ID in the session store Check the signature and expiry
How the credential is sent Usually a cookie (automatically, by the browser) Usually the Authorization header (by the code)
Logout, forced logout Deleting the session ends it immediately The token stays valid until exp
When permissions change Applied from the next request Applied when a new token is issued
With multiple servers They need a shared session store Any server with the same secret key can verify

With multiple servers

By default, sessions are kept in server memory. With two servers, if server A handles the login and server B handles the next request, server B doesn’t have that session. So a session store shared by all servers is used, such as Spring Session with Redis.

Tokens store nothing on the server, so any server holding the same secret key can verify them.

Logout

With sessions, once the server deletes the session, requests carrying that session ID are immediately no longer logged in.

With tokens, the server stores nothing, so it has no way to invalidate a token it has already issued. Even if the browser deletes the token, anyone who copied it can keep making requests with it until exp. That’s why tokens are given short lifetimes and paired with refresh tokens for getting new ones, which the next post covers.

Cookies and sessions

“Using cookies means using sessions” isn’t true. Cookies are a way to send the credential; sessions and tokens are ways to remember the login state, and the two are chosen separately. A JWT can be sent in an HttpOnly cookie, and a session ID can be sent in a header. Where to keep a token and how to send it is also in the next post.

Summary

Sessions Tokens
Where the login state is kept On the server Inside the token
How the server recognises the user Looks up the session ID Verifies the signature and reads the contents
Good fit The page and API are on the same server, and logouts must take effect immediately There are several servers, or apps and other services call the same API

Neither is simply better; the choice depends on how the servers are set up and how quickly a logout has to take effect.

item.title: Cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage
item.description: How cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage, the places a browser stores values, differ and how to use each.
item.content:encoded:
Reload a page and every value held in a JavaScript variable is gone. Values that need to survive a reload, such as a dark mode setting, a post being written or the login state, go in browser storage.

This post looks at how cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage differ and how to use each. Which of them should hold login information is covered in the next post.

Browser storage

Browser storage is space where the browser keeps values for each site. The values stay through reloads and page changes.

Description
Cookies Small values the server asks the browser to store, sent back to the server with every request
localStorage Storage read and written from JavaScript. Stays until cleared
sessionStorage Used the same way as localStorage, but cleared when the tab closes
IndexedDB A database for files and large amounts of data

This post covers cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage. localStorage and sessionStorage together are called Web Storage.

Web Storage

Usage

localStorage and sessionStorage share the same functions. They store keys and values in pairs.

Values are stored only as strings. Convert an object to a string with JSON.stringify to save it, and turn it back with JSON.parse when reading.

You can store about 5MB, and the exact limit varies a little between browsers.

Lifetime and sharing

Web Storage is kept separately for each origin. An origin is the protocol, domain and port together. https://app.example.com and http://app.example.com have different protocols, so they are different origins with separate storage.

Within one origin, the two stores differ in how long values last and whether tabs share them.

localStorage sessionStorage
Reload Kept Kept
Closing the tab Kept Cleared
Closing the browser Kept Cleared
Another tab on the same origin Reads and writes the same values Each tab has its own

Values that apply the same way in every tab and should still be there on the next visit, like dark mode, go in localStorage. Values that differ per tab and aren’t needed once the tab closes, like the current step of a multi-step form, go in sessionStorage.

Cookies

A cookie is a small value the server asks the browser to store. The browser sends its stored cookies along with every request to that server. The difference is that Web Storage is storage JavaScript reads and writes itself, while cookies are storage for exchanging values with the server.

How cookies travel

The server has a cookie stored with the Set-Cookie header of a response.

The browser stores the cookie, and puts it in the Cookie header of later requests to the same server.

The browser adds the Cookie header on its own. You don’t write it in your fetch or axios code. The same goes for page navigation, images and fetch requests.

A single cookie can be up to about 4KB. Since cookies go with every request, larger and more numerous cookies make every request larger.

Cookie attributes

Attributes follow the name=value in Set-Cookie, separated by ;.

Attribute What it does Example
Max-Age How many seconds until it’s deleted Max-Age=2592000 (30 days)
Expires The date it’s deleted Expires=Fri, 13 Nov 2026 09:00:00 GMT
Path Which paths it’s sent to Path=/ (every path)
Domain Which domains it’s sent to Domain=example.com (subdomains included)
  • Leave out both Max-Age and Expires and the cookie is deleted when the browser closes. This is called a session cookie. Session here means “while the browser is open”, which is a different thing from the login session in the next post.
  • Leave out Domain and the cookie is sent only to the domain that created it. With Domain=example.com, it’s also sent with requests to subdomains such as app.example.com and api.example.com.

Cookies in JavaScript

Cookies can also be read and written from JavaScript with document.cookie.

Reading it gives every cookie available to the page as one string in the form name=value; name=value. Getting one value means splitting that string yourself, so values used only by the page are easier to handle in Web Storage.

Cookie security attributes

Cookies often hold login information. So there are attributes that keep cookies from being stolen or used by someone else.

HttpOnly

XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is an attack where someone puts a script into something like a post’s content, so that it runs in the browsers of other users who open that page. The script runs with the same permissions as the site’s own code, so it can read localStorage and document.cookie and send them to the attacker’s server.

A cookie marked HttpOnly can’t be read from JavaScript. It doesn’t appear in document.cookie; it is only sent along with requests.

Even if an XSS script runs, it can’t read this cookie’s value. The site’s own code can’t read it either, so don’t mark values that JavaScript needs to read.

Secure

A cookie marked Secure is sent only with HTTPS requests. HTTP requests aren’t encrypted, so anyone who can see the request along the way sees the cookie value as is.

Browsers treat http://localhost during development as a secure address, so they store and send Secure cookies there too.

SameSite

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is an attack where, while a user is logged in, another site they open makes a request to the original site without them knowing. The browser adds cookies to requests automatically, so the server treats the request as coming from the logged-in user.

SameSite decides whether a cookie is sent with requests that start from another site. A site here is a wider unit than an origin. Two addresses are the same site if their protocol and registrable domain (a name registered with a domain registrar, like example.com) match.

Two addresses Origin Site
https://app.example.com, https://api.example.com Different Same
https://example.com, https://example.com:8080 Different Same
https://app.example.com, https://app.other.com Different Different
Value For requests that start from another site
Strict Not sent
Lax Sent only with GET requests that navigate to a page from a link
None Always sent. Must be paired with Secure

With Lax, arriving from a link on another site keeps the user logged in, while a fetch or form submission (POST) sent by another site’s code goes without the cookie. Strict doesn’t send the cookie even on the first page reached from another site’s link, so a logged-in user can end up looking at the login screen.

Chromium-based browsers such as Chrome treat a cookie without SameSite as Lax. This default differs between browsers, so writing it explicitly when creating the cookie makes it behave the same everywhere.

Sending cookies to an API on another address

If the page is served from https://app.example.com and the API from https://api.example.com, the two are different origins. In that case fetch and axios don’t put cookies in requests by default, and don’t store Set-Cookie from responses either.

To send cookies with requests to another origin, set an option.

credentials is the option that decides whether credentials such as cookies go with the request. The default for fetch is 'same-origin', which sends them only to the same origin; 'include' sends them to other origins too. axios’s withCredentials: true does the same.

The server has to allow it with response headers as well. Otherwise the browser blocks the response with a CORS error.

  • Put the page’s exact origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, not *. Requests sent with cookies can’t use *.
  • Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true means the page’s code may read the response to a request sent with cookies.

The two addresses in the example are different origins but the same site, so SameSite=Lax cookies are sent too. If the page and the API are on different sites (app.example.com and api.other.com), the cookie needs SameSite=None; Secure, and browsers that block other sites’ cookies by default, such as Safari and Firefox, may still not send it.

During development, a dev server proxy such as Vite’s can forward /api requests to the API server so the page and the API act as the same origin. Cookies then travel without any of the settings above.

Summary

Cookies localStorage sessionStorage
Who sets values Mostly the server (Set-Cookie) JavaScript JavaScript
Size About 4KB per cookie About 5MB per origin About 5MB per origin
Lifetime Until Max-Age or Expires; without them, until the browser closes Until cleared Until the tab closes
Kept separately by Domain and path Origin Origin and tab
Sent to the server automatically With every request No No
Readable from JavaScript Not if HttpOnly Yes Yes

Values the server needs on every request go in cookies, and values used only by the page go in Web Storage. Where to keep the values received at login depends on how safe each option is against XSS and CSRF, which the next post covers along with how login works.

item.title: Zustand and React Query
item.description: Splitting state into client state and server state, handling each with Zustand and React Query, and using the two together.
item.content:encoded:
The React hook basics post used props and useContext to pass values between components. When several components need to share the same value, you can manage it with a state management library instead of React’s built-in features. Data received from a server can likewise be managed with a library made for it.

This post covers two of those libraries, Zustand and React Query. It looks at how the two differ and how to use each.

Client state and server state

The values a page keeps fall into two kinds, depending on where the data is stored.

  • Client state: data stored only in the browser. Whether the sidebar is open, which tab is selected, what’s typed in the search box. It’s fine for it to disappear on reload, and the server doesn’t know about it.
  • Server state: data stored in the server’s database. The page fetches it and displays it. A list of posts, user details and order statistics are examples.

What makes server state different

Client state doesn’t change unless you change it. Server state does. While the page is showing the data it fetched, another user may write a post; the data on the server changes, and the data the page holds becomes out of date.

So server state comes with work that client state doesn’t have.

  • Showing whether it’s still loading or has failed
  • Requesting only once when several screens use the same data
  • Deciding the fetched data is out of date and requesting it again
  • Fetching related lists again after changing data

The two kinds of state are handled by different libraries.

Libraries Covered in this post
Client state Redux, Zustand, Jotai, etc. Zustand
Server state React Query, SWR, RTK Query, etc. React Query

Zustand

Zustand is a state management library for client state. It keeps values in a store outside the components, and several components take values from that store and share them.

Libraries that do the same job differ in how they gather values together.

  • Store-based: the app’s state is gathered in an object called a store. Redux and Zustand work this way. Redux sets a rule that values change through actions (objects describing what to do) and reducers (functions that take an action and produce the new state); Zustand changes them directly with functions inside the store.
  • Atom-based: an atom is the smallest unit, one that can’t be split further. Each value shared by several components is made into its own atom, and each component picks only the atoms it needs. Jotai works this way.

Which one is more convenient depends on how the shared values relate to each other.

Atom-based Store-based
How the values relate Each changes on its own Changing one changes others too
Example Theme, font size, sidebar open A cart’s item list, count and total

Changing the theme leaves the font size alone, so each value can simply be its own atom. In a cart, adding one item has to change the list, the count and the total together. With the three values and a function such as addItem in one store, changing all three when an item is added is handled in that one function.

Creating a store

A store is an object that gathers values and the functions that change them in one place. You create it with create.

  • set is the function that changes the store’s values. The object you pass is merged into the existing state. Unlike setState from useState, you don’t spread the remaining values in yourself.
  • If you need the previous value, pass a function: set((state) => ...).

Using it in a component

The useSidebarStore that create returns is a hook, starting with use like useState. Call it inside a component and pass a function that picks the value you need, and you get that value back.

The two components don’t need to be parent and child. Each takes what it needs from the store instead of receiving props, so the props drilling seen in the React hook basics post doesn’t happen.

Selectors

A function such as (state) => state.isOpen, which picks the value you need out of the store, is called a selector. A component re-renders only when the value its selector returns changes.

In the example above, pressing toggle changes isOpen and only Sidebar re-renders. The toggle function that SidebarButton picked is unchanged, so it doesn’t re-render.

Taking the whole store without a selector loses this benefit.

Picking values one at a time is all you need. Only when you pick several values bundled into one object or array is there something to watch for.

This selector makes a new object with { ... } every time it’s called. Zustand compares the selector’s result with the previous one using ===, and a new object is a different object every time even when the values inside are the same, so Zustand decides the value has changed. In Zustand v5, this repeats and can end in a Maximum update depth exceeded error.

In that case, wrap the selector in useShallow. Instead of comparing the object as a whole, useShallow compares the values inside one by one, and if they’re all the same it hands back the previous object.

Using it outside a component

Sometimes a store’s value has to be changed somewhere that isn’t a component. For example, when an API request function hits an error, you may want to record it in a store and have one place on the page show an error dialog based on that value.

Say the error store is created like this.

Here you can’t call useErrorStore((state) => state.setError) to get setError the way you would in a component. useErrorStore is a hook, and React hooks can only be called inside component functions; an API request function isn’t a component.

So Zustand attaches a function called getState to the hook that create makes. getState() returns the store’s current state object, and since it isn’t a hook, it can be called anywhere. The object it returns holds both the values and the functions.

fetchPosts below is a function that fetches the list of posts from the server address /api/posts. The other examples in this post use the same address.

Compared with useContext

Sharing values across several components is something useContext does too. There are two differences.

useContext Zustand
Setup Must wrap with a Provider Just create
What re-renders Every component using that Context when value changes Only components whose selected value changed

Here’s an example of the second difference: an app that shares the logged-in user (user) and the number of items in the cart (cartCount). UserName at the top of the page uses only user, and CartBadge uses only cartCount.

When an item is added to the cart and cartCount changes, this happens.

useContext Zustand
CartBadge Re-renders Re-renders
UserName Re-renders (even though user is unchanged) Doesn’t re-render

useContext only looks at whether the value object changed, so every component using that Context re-renders even when the value it uses is the same. Zustand compares what each selector returns and re-renders only the components whose value changed.

So values that rarely change, such as the logged-in user or the theme, are fine in useContext. For something that changes often and is shared by several components, such as the cart count, useContext re-renders components that don’t even use it every time, while Zustand re-renders only the components that use it.

React Query

React Query is a library that fetches server state, keeps it in a cache and manages when to fetch it again. Its current name is TanStack Query, and this post is based on v5.

How it differs from axios

axios and the browser’s fetch are HTTP clients. All they do is send requests to a server and receive responses (fetch and axios post). React Query doesn’t send requests itself. The function you hand it sends the request, and React Query manages when to request and where to keep the result.

axios, fetch React Query
What it does Sends requests and receives responses Keeps responses in a cache and decides when to request again
What it knows about Address, headers, request body Query keys, the cache, where the data is used on the page

That’s why the two are used together. In the code below, the part that sends the request is axios.

useQuery

  • queryKey: the name of this data. Covered below.
  • queryFn: the function that fetches the data. It just needs to return a Promise.
  • isPending: there is no data yet.
  • isError: the request failed. By default, a failed request is retried three more times before it gets here.

You don’t need separate useState values for loading and failure.

To use React Query, wrap the app once in a QueryClientProvider. The cache lives inside the QueryClient created here.

Query keys and the cache

A cache is storage that keeps fetched data so it can be used again later. React Query tells cache entries apart by their query key.

  • When several components use the same query key, only one request goes out. They all share the data it returns.
  • A query key is an array, and it includes the request’s conditions too, because different conditions mean different data.

If a value queryFn uses is left out of the query key, the key stays the same when the condition changes, and the data for the old condition keeps showing. Every value used inside queryFn goes in the query key.

staleTime and gcTime

Data in the cache has two timers.

  • staleTime: how long fetched data counts as fresh. After that, the data is stale (out of date).
  • gcTime: how long to wait, once no component uses the data any more, before removing it from the cache.
Default Longer Shorter
staleTime 0 Fewer requests, but old data is shown for that long even if the server has changed Always close to fresh, but more requests
gcTime 5 minutes Reopening a screen can show cached data right away, but uses more memory Uses less memory, but reopening loads from scratch

With the default staleTime of 0, data is stale as soon as it arrives. Stale data is requested again when:

  • a component using that query appears on screen
  • the browser window gets focus again
  • the network reconnects

While it’s being requested again, the data already in the cache is shown first. So isPending is false, and whether a request is in flight is shown by isFetching.

For data that rarely changes (code lists, settings), a longer staleTime cuts down requests. How long to set it depends on how often the data changes and whether showing old values for a moment is acceptable.

useMutation and invalidation

Requests that create, change or delete data use useMutation. Unlike useQuery, it doesn’t run when the component appears; it runs when you call mutate.

After a new post is written, the cached list of posts is out of date. That’s when you invalidate the query with invalidateQueries. To invalidate means to mark as no longer valid: it marks the cached data as stale and, if the page is currently using it, requests it again right away.

Invalidating with queryKey: ['posts'] targets every query that starts with ['posts']. ['posts', { page: 1 }] and ['posts', { page: 2 }] are invalidated together.

Compared with fetching in useEffect

Doing the same thing without React Query looks like this.

This code handles a single request for a single component. If another screen uses the same list it sends another request, it doesn’t refetch when the window regains focus, and refreshing the list after writing a post means wiring state together yourself. React Query handles all of this with one query key.

Name changes between v3 and v5

Up to v3 the package was called react-query; from v4 it’s @tanstack/react-query. When reading code in older projects, these names differ.

v3 (react-query) v5 (@tanstack/react-query)
useQuery('posts', fetchPosts, options) useQuery({ queryKey: ['posts'], queryFn: fetchPosts })
isLoading (no data yet) isPending
cacheTime gcTime
invalidateQueries('posts') invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['posts'] })
onSuccess, onError on useQuery Removed; still on useMutation

Using them together

When using both libraries, there’s one rule for deciding: if the data is stored only in the browser, it goes in Zustand; if it’s stored on the server, it goes in React Query.

Filter values and request conditions

Take a page where you pick a date range and see order statistics. The range the user picks lives only in the browser; the statistics for that range live on the server.

The range picker and the statistics component pass no props to each other. When the range picker calls setRange, things follow on like this.

enabled is an option that decides whether the query runs. When it’s false, no request is made. It keeps a bad request from going out when the range has been cleared and is empty.

Not copying server data into a store

Some code takes the data from useQuery and puts it into a Zustand store again in onSuccess or useEffect. The intent is to use it in several components, but it leaves the same data in two places, the cache and the store.

  • When invalidation brings new data into the cache, the copy in the store stays as it was.
  • Finding out which one is current means tracing through the code.

To use the data in several components, call useQuery with the same query key. Only one request goes out and the cache is shared. Wrapping it in a hook like useOrderStats above means the query key isn’t written out in several places.

Real-time data

Not all server state suits React Query. React Query is built around data you request. Data the server keeps pushing over a WebSocket, such as chat messages or live prices, has no moment when you request it.

For data like this, you either put incoming messages into a Zustand store for the page to subscribe to, or change the React Query cache directly with queryClient.setQueryData. If a page fetches the initial list with a request and then receives only changes over the WebSocket, changing the cache keeps it all in one place; if a page is filled only by messages with no request, keeping it in a store is simpler.

Summary

Zustand React Query
State it handles Client state Server state
Where the data is stored Browser Server
How values change set Request the server, then invalidate
What re-renders Components whose selected value changed Components using that query key
Examples Sidebar open, selected tab, chosen range Post list, user details, statistics by range

Sending requests is the job of axios or fetch; caching the results and deciding when to fetch again is React Query’s job. Values that live only in the browser go in Zustand, and when you use such a value as a request condition, you put it in the query key.

item.title: fetch and axios
item.description: How to send requests from browser code to a server with fetch and axios, how they differ, and what axios instances and interceptors are for.
item.content:encoded:
The CSR post said that with CSR the browser receives an empty HTML page, and then JS fetches data from an API and builds the page. This post is about that “fetches data from an API” part. It looks at how fetch and axios, the two tools used to send requests from browser code to a server, differ, and how to use each.

The await and Promises in the example code are covered in the Synchronous and asynchronous post.

HTTP clients

An HTTP client is a tool that sends HTTP requests to a server and receives the responses. When you type a URL into the address bar, the browser does this; in code, you call an HTTP client function to do the same.

The examples in this post use a server address, /api/posts, that returns a list of blog posts. A request and its response look like this.

What the status codes mean is covered in the HTTP status codes post. For this post, all you need is that 2xx means success and 4xx and 5xx mean failure.

There are several HTTP clients for JavaScript.

Description
fetch A function built into browsers and Node.js 18+
axios The most widely used HTTP client library
ky, ofetch, etc. Libraries that wrap fetch to make it as convenient as axios

This post covers fetch and axios.

fetch

GET requests

  • res is short for response. Once fetch(url) receives a response, it returns a Response object holding the whole thing: the status code (res.status), the headers (res.headers) and the body.
  • The body hasn’t been read yet. Calling res.json() reads it and turns it into a JavaScript value. Reading the body also takes time, so res.json() doesn’t hand back the value right away; it returns a Promise, and you await it to get the value.
  • posts is the body taken out that way: the list of posts.

Reading the response body

Logged with console.log, res looks like this.

The status code and headers can be read right away, but the body is a stream of data (ReadableStream) that may still be downloading. res.json() reads that body to the end and, in the same step, turns the text it read, '[{"id":1,"title":"First post"}]', into the JavaScript value [{ id: 1, title: 'First post' }].

Which function reads the body depends on its format.

Function Returns Used for
res.json() A JavaScript object or array JSON responses
res.text() A string HTML, plain text
res.blob() File data Images, file downloads

The body can be read only once. After that, bodyUsed becomes true and trying to read it again throws an error. So you call just one of the three.

POST requests

To send data, put the method, headers and body in the second argument.

  • body must be a string, so the object is converted with JSON.stringify.
  • The Content-Type header tells the server the body is JSON.

Checking the response

fetch counts it as success as long as the server sends back a response. A 404 or 500 is still a response, so it doesn’t throw. That’s why you check the status code yourself.

res.ok is true when the status code is 200–299. res.status holds the status code as a number.

fetch throws when no response arrives: the connection dropped, the server address is wrong, or the browser blocked the response because of a CORS error.

axios

axios isn’t built in like fetch, so you install the package.

GET requests

axios’s res is the whole response too. If the body is JSON, axios reads it ahead of time, turns it into a JavaScript value and puts it in res.data. So res.data is the list of posts, and there’s no separate res.json() call.

POST requests

Pass an object as the second argument and axios turns it into a JSON string and adds the Content-Type: application/json header.

Handling errors

axios throws when the response’s status code isn’t 2xx. So failures are handled in one place, try...catch.

  • error.response holds the response the server sent back. It’s empty when no response arrived.
  • axios.isAxiosError(error) checks whether the error came from axios. In TypeScript you need this check before using error.response.

Compared with fetch

fetch axios
Install Not needed Install the package
Response body Call await res.json() yourself Already in res.data
Data to send Set JSON.stringify and Content-Type yourself Pass the object as is
4xx and 5xx responses Treated as success; check res.ok yourself Throws an error
Shared settings Set on every request Set once on an instance
Intercepting requests and responses No Interceptors
Timeout Pass AbortSignal.timeout() yourself timeout option

The last three rows are the main reasons to use axios. They come next.

axios instances

Most of the APIs an app calls live on the same server and use the same headers and timeout. To avoid repeating those settings on every request, you use axios.create to make an axios with the settings fixed. This is called an instance: one concrete copy made from axios. You can make several instances from the same axios, each with different settings.

  • baseURL: the address put in front of every request path. If the development and production servers have different addresses, this is the only value you change.
  • timeout: the longest time, in milliseconds, to wait for a response. The default is 0, which means waiting with no limit. A short value gives up quickly on a server that doesn’t answer; too short, and slow but healthy requests fail too.

If there are two servers, make two instances and use each for its server.

Interceptors

An interceptor is something that catches things on their way through. In axios, it’s a function that runs before every request sent through an instance goes out, or before every response reaches your code. It puts work you’d otherwise repeat on every request in one place.

Request interceptors

An example that adds the logged-in user’s token to the header of every request.

config is this request’s settings (address, headers and so on). The request goes out with the config the function returns.

Response interceptors

An example that sends the user to the login page when the login has expired and a 401 comes back.

  • The first function receives 2xx responses; the second receives errors.
  • Returning Promise.reject(error) from the second function passes the error on to the catch of the code that made the request. Shared handling goes in the interceptor, and handling that differs per screen goes in each catch.

To show an error alert from one place, have the response interceptor record the error in a state management library’s store, and display that value in one spot on the page.

Interceptors are also used to return only the body of a successful response.

This saves taking out res.data wherever you make a request. The trade-off is that values received through this instance no longer carry the status code or headers.

Summary

fetch axios
What it does Sends HTTP requests to a server and receives responses Same
What counts as failure Any response is success; check the status code yourself Anything other than 2xx throws
Shared settings None Instances (axios.create)
Shared handling None Interceptors

If you only make requests in a few places and need no shared settings, fetch alone is enough. If many places call the same server and you want token and error handling in one place, axios instances and interceptors cut that work down. You can also build the same structure on fetch yourself, or use a library such as ky.

item.title: Synchronous and asynchronous
item.description: How JavaScript handles slow work such as server requests without waiting on it, going through callbacks, Promises and async/await in turn.
item.content:encoded:
Synchronous and asynchronous execution come up in every language whenever a task involves waiting: reading a file, querying a database, calling a server. The async, await and then you meet when using fetch, axios or React Query in JavaScript are all ways of dealing with that waiting.

This post looks at how synchronous and asynchronous code differ in browser JavaScript, and how to write asynchronous code.

Synchronous and asynchronous

Synchronous execution starts a task only after the previous one has finished. Code runs line by line from top to bottom, and the next line doesn’t start until the current one is done.

Asynchronous execution starts a slow task and moves on to the next one without waiting for it to finish. When the task is done, its result is picked up and handled then.

setTimeout doesn’t stand still for that second. It hands over the function to run later and moves straight on to the next line, so 2 is printed first.

Why the browser needs asynchrony

In the browser, JavaScript does one thing at a time. That single flow of execution runs your code, draws the page, and handles clicks and scrolling.

So if it waited synchronously for something slow, the whole page would freeze in the meantime. The code below does nothing but spin in a loop for 3 seconds.

If server requests worked like this, the page would lock up while waiting for every response. That’s why network requests such as fetch and timers such as setTimeout are asynchronous. The waiting is left to the browser, and JavaScript carries on with other work in the meantime.

Callbacks

Passing a function to be run after an asynchronous task finishes is called a callback. The function passed to setTimeout above is a callback.

When you chain asynchronous tasks that must run in order using only callbacks, each next callback goes inside the previous one, so the code keeps indenting further. Errors also have to be handled separately at every step. Promises came along to ease this.

Promise

A Promise is an object that lets you receive the result of an asynchronous task later. The name means exactly that: there’s no result yet, but you get a promise of one up front. An asynchronous function can’t hand back its result right away, so it hands back a Promise instead.

The examples in this post assume a server address, /api/posts, that returns a list of blog posts. fetch is a function built into the browser for sending requests to a server.

States

A Promise is always in one of three states.

State Meaning
pending The task hasn’t finished yet
fulfilled The task finished and there is a result
rejected The task failed and there is an error

Once it moves from pending to fulfilled or rejected, it never changes again.

then and catch

You receive the result by passing a function to then, and the error by passing one to catch.

  • The function passed to then runs with the result once the Promise is fulfilled.
  • then returns another Promise, so calls can be chained. Whatever one then returns is passed to the next. If it returns a Promise, the next then waits for that Promise to finish and receives its result.
  • res and posts are just parameter names, so any names will do. What res and res.json() are is covered in the fetch and axios post.
  • If anything along the way fails, the remaining thens are skipped and it goes to catch.

Unlike callbacks, the steps read from top to bottom in order, and errors are handled in one place, catch.

async and await

async and await are syntax for writing Promise code so it reads top to bottom like synchronous code. async is short for asynchronous; putting it before a function marks it as an asynchronous function. await means what it says: wait.

  • await waits until the Promise is fulfilled and takes out its result. res holds the response object, not a Promise.
  • An async function always returns a Promise. return posts becomes a Promise fulfilled with posts.

Getting the result out

The result of a function that returns a Promise, such as fetch, is taken out with either await or then.

Without either one, you’re left with the Promise instead of the result. The request still goes to the server, but you can’t use the response, and if it fails try...catch can’t catch it.

How async and await relate

Relation Rule
A function that uses await Needs async; without it, it’s a syntax error. At the top level of a module file, await works without async
await inside an async function Optional

An async function returns a Promise even without await. But async is there so you can use await inside the function, so a function with no await doesn’t get it.

Inside and outside an async function

Seen from outside, an async function is asynchronous; inside, it behaves as if it were synchronous.

  • Inside: on reaching await, it waits for the result and then moves to the next line. It reads like synchronous code running one line after another.
  • Outside: the code that called the function doesn’t wait and moves straight on to its next line.

So even while await is waiting, the page doesn’t freeze; it keeps handling clicks and drawing.

Handling errors

If a Promise you await is rejected, an error is thrown on that line. You catch it with try...catch, the same as in synchronous code.

Sending several requests together

When you send two unrelated requests and await them one at a time, the second request isn’t sent until the first response arrives.

Promise.all takes several Promises and makes one Promise that, once they’re all fulfilled, gives back their results as an array. All the requests are sent first and then waited on together, so in the end you only wait for the slowest one.

  • If any one fails, Promise.all fails right away. If you want the other results even when some requests fail, use Promise.allSettled. Each result then says whether it was fulfilled or rejected.
  • If a later request needs an earlier result (fetching a user’s posts with that user’s ID), they can’t be sent together; await them one at a time.

Summary

How you get the result Error handling
Callback Pass a function to run when done Separately at each step
Promise then catch
async/await Take the value out with await try...catch

All three are ways of not freezing the page while slow work is waited on. fetch, axios and React Query all return Promises, so in code you mostly handle them with async and await.

item.title: React hook basics
item.description: Starting from the fact that a component function runs again when state changes, when and how to use the six basic React hooks.
item.content:encoded:
The CSR post said that with CSR the browser’s JS builds the page. In a React app the pieces that do that are components, and the functions that let a component remember values or do work after the screen is drawn are hooks. This post covers the six basic hooks you use most, and props, which is how components pass values to each other.

Components and rendering

A component is a function that returns the JSX to show on screen.

Pressing this button doesn’t change the number, for two reasons.

  • Changing count doesn’t tell React that the screen needs redrawing.
  • Even if it redrew, Counter() would run from the top and go back to let count = 0.

To change the screen in React you have to change a value React keeps for you: state. When state changes, React runs the component function again. This is called rendering.

Every hook in this post builds on this order. In particular, on every render the function runs from the top, and the variables, objects and functions inside it are created anew. That’s why useRef, useMemo and useCallback exist.

useState

A value that survives past the end of a render, and that redraws the screen when you change it.

Part Meaning
useState(0) The initial value. Used only on the first render
count The value for this render
setCount A function that changes the value and triggers a re-render

Values don’t change immediately

Calling setCount doesn’t change count in the function that’s currently running. The new value shows up on the next render.

Updating from the previous value

For the same reason, writing this to add two at once only adds one.

To update based on the previous value, pass a function. React passes in the value just before.

Objects and arrays

React decides whether to redraw by checking whether the new value is the same object as the old one. If it’s the same array, React treats it as unchanged even if its contents changed.

... is the spread syntax. It lays out the contents of an array or object one by one in place. So [...items] is a new array with the same contents, and { ...user } is a new object with the same fields.

Goal Changing the original (avoid) Making a new one
Add push [...items, item]
Remove splice items.filter((x) => x.id !== id)
Update items[i] = … items.map((x) => x.id === id ? { ...x, name } : x)
Sort sort [...items].sort(…), items.toSorted(…)
Change an object field user.name = … { ...user, name }

It’s easy to miss that sort reorders the original array. Calling sort directly on an array of data from the server also changes the order for other screens that use the same data.

props

Props are the values a parent component passes to a child component. A component is a function, so props are that function’s arguments.

Property Meaning
Read-only A child doesn’t change the props it receives. If it needs changing, the parent that owns the value changes it
Re-render with the parent When the parent re-renders, the child re-renders too, even if its props are the same

Function props

When a child needs to change a parent’s value, the parent passes a function as a prop and the child calls it.

PlusButton doesn’t know about count; it only reports that it was pressed by calling onPlus(). Parent is what changes the state, and the new count reaches the screen when Parent re-renders.

Data in React flows one way like this. Values go down as props, and events go up as function calls. To find where a value changes, you only need to look at the one component that holds it as state.

Lifting state up

When two sibling components need the same value, move that state to their common parent and hand it to both as props. This is called lifting state up.

If SearchInput kept keyword as its own state, ResultList couldn’t know it. When their parent SearchPage holds the state, both receive it as props.

props drilling

As state moves upward, you end up with intermediate components that take props they never use, just to pass them on to one component at the bottom. This is called props drilling.

A few levels are fine. As it gets deeper, the intermediate components have to know about props that have nothing to do with them, and renaming a prop or changing its type means editing every file it passes through. At that point you can use useContext below, or manage the value with a state management library.

useEffect

Registers work to run after the screen is drawn. Work that has nothing to do with producing the render result goes here: API calls, timers, event subscriptions, direct DOM manipulation.

Dependency array

The array passed as the second argument decides when the effect runs again.

Dependency array When it runs
None After every render
[] Once, when the component first appears
[id] Once at first, then whenever id changes

Put every prop, state value and variable the effect uses into the array. If one is missing, the effect keeps using its old value. ESLint’s react-hooks/exhaustive-deps rule points out missing ones.

Cleanup function

If an effect returns a function, React calls it before running the effect again and when the component leaves the screen. It’s used to cancel timers and subscriptions.

In development mode with StrictMode, effects run, clean up, and run again. This is to surface a missing cleanup right away; production builds run them once. It’s why APIs get called twice during development.

When you don’t need an effect

Values you can calculate from props or state should be calculated during rendering, without an effect and extra state.

In practice, API calls are often left to a library such as React Query rather than written with useEffect by hand. It handles loading and error states, caching and refetching for you.

useRef

A value that survives past the end of a render but doesn’t trigger a re-render when it changes. You read and write it through ref.current.

Use Example
Holding a DOM element Focusing an input, scrolling to a position
Keeping a value unrelated to the screen A timer id, a previous value, whether a request is in flight
Plain variable useState useRef
Survives to the next render No. Created anew each time Yes Yes
Re-renders when changed No Yes No
When the new value is visible Immediately Next render Immediately

Use useState for values that must show on screen, and useRef for values you only need to remember.

useMemo and useCallback

Objects and functions inside a component are created anew on every render. Even with the same contents, a newly created object counts as a different object from the previous one.

useMemo remembers a computed result, and useCallback remembers a function. If the values in the dependency array haven’t changed, they return what was made before.

useCallback(fn, deps) is the same as useMemo(() => fn, deps). The thing being remembered just happens to be a function.

When they’re needed

Case Example
The calculation is heavy Sorting or filtering a list of thousands of items
The result is passed on as something another place compares A useEffect dependency array, props of a child wrapped in React.memo

The second case is the options example above. Without remembering it, the effect runs on every render, or a child wrapped in React.memo sees its props as changed and re-renders every time.

When they’re not needed

  • Light calculations such as filtering a short array or joining strings
  • When the result is used directly on screen and isn’t passed anywhere that compares it

In these cases the cost of remembering (comparing dependencies, keeping the old value) plus longer code outweighs the gain. Adding it doesn’t change behavior, but putting it on every value makes it hard to see where it really matters. With React Compiler, this memoization is inserted automatically at build time, so you need to add it by hand less often.

Don’t change the original inside

When sorting inside useMemo, don’t change the original array either.

In JS, putting an array in a variable or passing it around doesn’t copy it. Several names simply point at the same single array.

sort doesn’t create a new array; it reorders the array itself. So in the first snippet above, data.sort(…) isn’t a value used only inside useMemo; it changes the original array data points to.

If data is server data from a library such as React Query, that array is the very array the library keeps in its cache. Any other screen using the same data receives the reordered array as well. With two screens that sort differently, each overwrites the other’s order, and the result depends on which one renders first.

Sorting a copy made with [...data] leaves the original alone. data.toSorted(…) does the same thing: it returns a new sorted array and leaves the original unchanged.

Method Changes the original Use instead
sort Yes [...arr].sort(), arr.toSorted()
reverse Yes [...arr].reverse(), arr.toReversed()
splice Yes filter, arr.toSpliced()
push, pop, shift, unshift Yes [...arr, item], arr.slice(…)
map, filter, slice, concat No Fine as is

useContext

Solves the props drilling above. Put a value in once at the top, and components below take it out directly without going through the ones in between.

When the Provider’s value changes, every component that uses it re-renders. That makes it a good fit for values used in many places that don’t change often, such as the logged-in user, the theme or the language. When a value shared by many components changes often, you can manage it with a state management library such as Zustand, so that components that don’t use it aren’t re-rendered as well.

Rules of hooks

Hooks aren’t functions you can call from anywhere. React sets two rules for them. They apply not only to the hooks in this post but also to hooks from libraries and hooks you write yourself.

Only inside components

Call hooks only inside a component function or another hook. A regular function can’t call them.

The values a hook remembers are stored on the component that is currently rendering. A regular function has no rendering component, so there is nowhere to store them.

At the top of the component

Call hooks at the top of the component function. If you need a condition, write it after the hooks.

If a useEffect should only run under some condition, put the condition inside the useEffect.

ESLint’s react-hooks/rules-of-hooks rule points out code that breaks either rule.

Custom hooks

A function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks is itself a hook. You write one, like useLoginUser in this post, to wrap a combination of hooks that several components use. The use prefix is how ESLint recognises it as a hook and checks the rules above.

Summary

Hook What it does Re-renders
useState Remembers a value and redraws the screen when it changes When changed
useEffect Runs work after the screen is drawn No (yes if it changes state inside)
useRef Remembers a value or a DOM element No
useMemo Remembers a computed result No
useCallback Remembers a function No
useContext Takes out a value passed from above When the value changes

item.title: CSR vs SSR
item.description: Covers the difference between CSR, where the browser builds a page's HTML, and SSR, where the server builds it, and which one the framework you use belongs to.
item.content:encoded:
What you see on screen is ultimately HTML. Whether the browser builds that HTML, or the server builds it and sends it is what separates CSR from SSR. This post covers how each one’s requests flow, how they differ, and which one the framework you use belongs to.

Rendering

Rendering is turning data into the HTML that appears on screen. Even for one page such as /history/12, the record data has to be made into HTML with a heading and a table.

Name Where the HTML is built
CSR Client-Side Rendering The browser, as the JS runs
SSR Server-Side Rendering The server, for every request, before sending it

Request flow

CSR

A React app built with Vite works this way. The dist from Nginx part 1 is what it produces.

  1. The browser requests /history/12, and Nginx sends index.html.
  2. index.html has no content, only the line that loads the JS file.
  3. The browser downloads and runs the JS, and the JS calls /api/history/12 to get the data.
  4. The JS uses that data to build the page inside <div id="root">.

The page appears only after step 4. During steps 1 to 3 the user sees a blank page or a spinner.

All the server does is send files. It can send the same index.html for any address, and the JS builds the page that matches the address. The try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html from Nginx part 1 does exactly this.

SSR

Frameworks such as Next.js and Nuxt work this way. The server that receives requests runs on Node.

  1. The browser requests /history/12, and the Node server receives it.
  2. The Node server calls the API itself to get the data.
  3. The Node server builds HTML filled with that data and sends it.
  4. The browser shows the HTML it received right away.
  5. The JS then downloads and runs, and wires up behavior such as clicks on the page that’s already showing.

The page appears at step 4, because the server has already done the API call and built the HTML before sending it.

Hydration

Step 5 of SSR is called hydration. The HTML the server sent can only be looked at; pressing a button does nothing. Only after the JS runs and attaches events to the existing HTML does it behave like a CSR app.

So SSR still downloads JS. The difference is that the page shows first, without waiting for the JS. After hydration, moving between pages is handled in the browser, just as with CSR.

Checking with the page source

To check which one a page uses, open View page source (Ctrl + U) in the browser. The page source is the HTML exactly as the server sent it, before any JS runs.

Page source Approach
Empty, like <div id="root"></div>, with none of the text on screen CSR
The text on screen is in the HTML SSR, or SSG below

The Elements tab in the developer tools shows the result after JS has run, so even a CSR page shows all its content there. To tell them apart, look at the page source, not Elements.

Differences

CSR SSR
Where the HTML is built The browser The server (Node)
The first HTML received No content Contains the content
When the first page appears After the JS runs and the API call finishes Right after the HTML arrives
Moving between pages Changes instantly in the browser Same as CSR after hydration
Search engines, link previews May not be able to read the content Read the content in the HTML
Server Only needs to send files (Nginx) A Node server that builds HTML for every request
Server load Light Rendering cost on every request

First page

With CSR, the larger the JS files and the slower the API, the later the first page appears. In the meantime the user sees a blank page. With SSR, the HTML response is delayed by the time the server spends calling the API, but the content shows as soon as it arrives.

Moving between pages

With CSR, once the JS has loaded, moving to another menu doesn’t fetch new HTML. The JS changes only the page and fetches only the data it needs from the API, so navigation is fast. An app that shows many screens by swapping content within one HTML page like this is called an SPA (Single Page Application).

Search engines and link previews

Search engines, and the previews that appear when you paste a link into a messenger, read the HTML the server sent. With CSR the HTML is empty, so they sometimes can’t read the content, title or image. Google sometimes runs the JS to read the page, but places such as messenger previews usually read only the HTML.

Server and deployment

CSR SSR
Build output HTML, JS and CSS files (dist) A server app run with Node
Deployment Put the files on Nginx Run the Node server as a container
Nginx’s role Serve the files and forward /api to the backend Forward requests to the Node server

CSR doesn’t add another server. With SSR the frontend becomes a server too, so there is one more process to run and keep an eye on.

SSG

SSG (Static Site Generation) builds the HTML ahead of time, at build time. When a request comes in, it only sends the prebuilt file.

When the HTML is built Server
CSR After the request, in the browser Only sends files
SSR On every request, on the server A Node server
SSG Once, at build time Only sends files

This blog uses SSG. When a post is published, the build creates the HTML for each post, and GitHub Pages only sends those files. That’s why the page source contains the whole post, and why the server, as with CSR, only needs the files.

The trade-off is that anything changed after the build needs another build to show up. It suits content that doesn’t change often, such as posts, and doesn’t suit pages that show different data to each user.

By framework

Here is where the frameworks in common use fall.

Framework Approach
React or Vue built with Vite CSR. The build output is static files in dist
Next.js (React), Nuxt (Vue) SSR by default, switchable to SSG or CSR page by page
Astro SSG by default, with SSR for the pages that need it. This blog is built with Astro
Spring with Thymeleaf or JSP SSR. The Java server builds the HTML and sends it

The same React is CSR when built with Vite and SSR when used on top of Next.js. What decides the approach isn’t the UI library but the framework around it.

The setup from Nginx part 1, where one Java app served both pages and the API, is SSR in the Thymeleaf or JSP style. Splitting those pages out into React turned them into CSR, and that’s why a separate Nginx to serve the frontend files became necessary.

Choosing

Page Fits Why
An admin screen used after logging in CSR It never needs to appear in search results, and Nginx alone is enough as the server
A blog or documentation site SSG The content rarely changes and should appear in search results
Shop product pages, news SSR The content changes often but still needs to appear in search results and link previews

An admin screen at work being CSR fits these criteria. You have to log in to use it, so it doesn’t need to show up in search engines, and although the first page is a little slower, moving around is fast once you’re in.

Frameworks such as Next.js can mix SSR, SSG and CSR page by page within one app. It isn’t a matter of picking just one, but of deciding, for each page, where its HTML gets built.

item.title: HTTP status codes and where an error came from
item.description: Covers what status codes like 404 Not Found mean, and how to use the developer tools to find where an error on the page came from.
item.content:encoded:
When the browser sends a request, the server puts a three-digit number at the very start of its response. That number is the status code. This post covers what the common status codes mean, and how to find where an error came from when one shows up on the page.

Status codes

The first line of a response looks like this.

Part Value Meaning
Protocol HTTP/1.1 The version of the protocol in use
Status code 404 How the request was handled
Reason phrase Not Found A human-readable name for the status code

The numbers and names are defined by the HTTP specification (currently RFC 9110). So every server uses 404 with the same meaning: “what you asked for wasn’t found”. Programs look only at the number; the name is there for people.

The 1xx to 5xx classes

The first digit sorts status codes into five classes. Even for a code you’ve never seen, the first digit tells you whether it succeeded and where the problem is.

Class Meaning Where to look
1xx A notice that processing continues Rarely seen. Mainly 101 when a connection switches to WebSocket
2xx Success Nothing wrong
3xx Redirection. A response telling the browser to request another address. 304 is a little different: it means use the stored copy Redirect settings, caching
4xx The request was wrong or not allowed The request. Address, values, login state, permissions
5xx The request was fine but the server couldn’t handle it The server. Backend logs, Nginx logs

Common status codes

2xx

Code Name When
200 OK A request such as a read or an update succeeded and there is a response body
201 Created A request that creates something (POST) succeeded
204 No Content It succeeded but there’s no body to return. Common for deletes

3xx

Code Name When
301 Moved Permanently The address has changed for good; go to the new one. The http → https redirect in Nginx part 2
302 Found Go to another address, this time only. Sending a user who isn’t logged in to the login page
304 Not Modified Nothing changed; use your stored copy. Not an error

A 3xx response carries the address to go to in the Location header. The browser requests that address next, so the developer tools show two lines for one request.

4xx

Code Name When
400 Bad Request The request values are wrong. Malformed JSON, a missing required value, a value of the wrong type
401 Unauthorized It isn’t known who is asking. Not logged in, no token, an expired token
403 Forbidden It’s known who is asking, but they aren’t allowed to make this request
404 Not Found Nothing exists at that address
405 Method Not Allowed The address exists but the method is wrong. A GET sent to an address that only takes POST
413 Content Too Large The request body is too large. A big file upload

5xx

Code Name When
500 Internal Server Error The backend threw an exception while handling the request
502 Bad Gateway A proxy in between (Nginx) didn’t get a valid response from the backend
503 Service Unavailable The server can’t take requests for now. Maintenance, overload
504 Gateway Timeout A proxy in between ran out of time waiting for the backend

Similar codes compared

401 and 403

Both mean “no”, but for different reasons.

401 403
Meaning It isn’t known who is asking It’s known who is asking, but it isn’t allowed
Common cause Not logged in, expired token A regular user calling an admin API
Fix Log in again Get the permission, or use an account that has it
